title: Eloelo's Dolphin AI Bets Budget Is No Longer Storytelling's Gatekeeper
excerpt: At TechSparks, Eloelo founder Saurabh Pandey argued that Dolphin AI's multi-shot production can cut the cost that kept big Indian stories off screen, as creators built about 15,000 videos in eight days.
body:
• Eloelo Group founder and CEO Saurabh Pandey showcased Dolphin AI at TechSparks, arguing that AI production can remove budget as the gatekeeper that decides which Indian stories get made.
  • Dolphin AI, first unveiled at FICCI FRAMES 2026 on September 29, uses multi-shot planning to preserve characters, voices, props and locations across a production, addressing AI video's usual 8 to 10 second continuity limit.
  • Eloelo says roughly 15,000 videos were built on Dolphin AI in about eight days through organic discovery, and the group produced more than 5,000 original dramas through Story TV while testing over 100,000 creatives a month.
  • For creators: Dolphin AI is currently on a waitlist with invite codes released in batches at trydolphin.ai, free early credits are available for first videos, and a credit-based pricing model will follow.

When James Cameron's Avatar reached cinemas in the late 2000s, many Indian viewers wondered why India was not making films on that scale. Saurabh Pandey, founder and CEO of Eloelo Group, told an audience at the 17th edition of TechSparks that the question is about to lose its force, according to YourStory. His answer is Dolphin AI, Eloelo's AI video creation tool.

Eloelo is a Bengaluru-based live social entertainment platform launched in 2020 by former Flipkart executives Pandey and Akshay Dubey. At TechSparks, Pandey argued that budgets, not talent, have decided which stories reach the screen.

The end of the budget bottleneck

In the visual effects era, Pandey said, filmmaking belonged to whoever had the money. A storyteller with a period drama in mind could not afford the visuals it demanded. Production usually consumes 50 to 60% of revenue in this category, squeezing distribution budgets and unit economics, and cutting those production costs gives creator imagination room to work.

Distribution has also changed. It is now largely algorithmic, Pandey said, so a creator in India competes for attention in the United States or Europe on the same footing as anyone else. That combination is the basis for his claim that India can move from consuming content to exporting it.

"I firmly believe AI is going to lead to a world of infinite content. With Dolphin AI, we hope India becomes the hub for the Orange Economy and moves from being one of the world's largest consumers of content to one of the largest exporters of content."

— Saurabh Pandey, Founder and CEO, Eloelo Group

Built from Eloelo's own production problem

Dolphin AI was first unveiled during Pandey's keynote at FICCI FRAMES 2026 in Mumbai on September 29, according to AdTechToday's launch report. It was born from Eloelo's own operations: through Story TV, the group has produced more than 5,000 original dramas and tests more than 100,000 creatives every month.

Most AI video tools lose context beyond 8 to 10 seconds. Dolphin's multi-shot planning and continuity systems are designed to preserve characters, voices, wardrobes, props, locations and visual language across a whole production rather than generating each shot independently, according to the company. Its Film Studio feature turns a script into a structured production, identifying characters, locations and props and creating reusable visual, voice and wardrobe assets. Dolphin also supports the Model Context Protocol, allowing clients including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Cursor to access its functions.

Creators can join the waitlist at trydolphin.ai, the site linked in Eloelo's launch announcement. Access is currently by invite codes released in batches, with free early credits so creators can make their first videos before credit-based pricing arrives.

Micro-drama is the immediate market

Pandey pointed to micro-drama as proof of demand. In India, he said, the top four or five micro-drama players together are running at more than Rs 5,000 crore, a level reached in just 18 months. Eloelo launched about 200 new micro-dramas last month, roughly five or six a night, and works with around 90 production houses.

He expects platforms to consolidate to two or three heavily funded players holding 70 to 75% of the market, as happened in food delivery, quick commerce, ecommerce and ride-hailing. The opportunity, he argued, is on the supply side: founders should build lean AI studios, with a handful of writers, editors, promo producers and a line producer, feeding micro-dramas, OTT content and exportable intellectual property to the big platforms.

What to watch

Pandey advised writers wary of AI to use it as a brainstorming partner and ship more, noting that an AI Ramayana exists but a spectacular AI Mahabharata has not yet been made. Eloelo has grown from one platform to five, he said, and an IPO is not planned anytime soon. Whether Dolphin can convert free credits into paid use will decide if the gatekeeper argument holds.
nri_angle: Algorithmic distribution lets Indian creators compete for US and European audiences on the same footing, and Dolphin AI's waitlist offers diaspora creators a low-cost way to test exportable Indian stories.
author: Diaspora Desk
